SHORT HISTORY OF THE DELTA CHAPTER
By Richard M. Haywood, Delta '54
"THE DELTA CHAPTER-"The Branch
I of Psi Epsilon"-was established on No
vember 11, 1837, the first chapter of the
fraternity, after the founding Theta Chap
ter at Union College. Less than five years
before, in 1832, New York University had
been founded.
During the first 25 years of the Delta's
existence, its members met in various loca
tions around New York University, as
there was no
Chapter House. During meet
ings there were
literary exercises, a tradition
which has been continued to ihis day. In
the period 1844-59, there were
joint meet
ings with the Lambda Chapter, which the
Delta had helped to estabhsh in 1842. Close
connections between the two chapters have
existed ever since.
During this early period the Delta pro
duced several alumni who had very dis
tinguished careers in later life, thereby es
tablishing the principle that the Delta
should not only serve Psi Upsilon and the
University but also society as a whole.
William F. Morgan, Delta '65, was the
first president of the executive council, in
1869.
The Civil War and consequent deple
tion of the active membership of the Chap
ter was the first of many such crises which
the Delta has had to face. However,
through the efforts of both graduate and
undergraduate members, by 1875 the
Chapter had regained its former strength.
The period 1875-94 witnessed a continual
growth. Charles M. Kingsley, Delta '83,
was a member of the Executive Council
from 1884 to 1901. With the passing years
many other Delta men have served on the
Executive Council�probably more than
any other chapter.
In 1893, the University authorities made
the decision to move the academic college
to University Heights in the Bronx. The
Delta moved uptown with it and rented
its first Chapter House on the new cam
pus in the autumn of 1894.
In January, 1897, the Delta Corpora
tion was brought into existence, with
power to raise money for a new
Chapter
House, and later to hold title to it and
maintain it upon completion. The Delta
Corporation originally had ten (now nine)
directors, with general membership open
to all Delta alumni. The Delta has always
been proud of its alumni, who have sup
ported and aided it in good times and bad
and who have helped to make the Chap
ter the strong, thriving institution it is
today. There are some alumni who have
not missed a Yule Log ceremony, initia
tion, or Delta Day Dinner for over half a
century. It is not possible to mention all
of the brothers who participated in the
creative building of this period. Never to
be forgotten for their help are, William M.
Kingsley, Delta '83, and John V. Irwin,
Delta '94, who wrote "The Branch of Psi
Upsilon," history of the Delta.
In November, 1899, the present Chap
ter House was dedicated, having been
built by the generous contributions of many
brethren, with especially strong support
coming from the late Brother Frank Jay
Gould, Delta '99, who through the years
gave so much to the Delta and to the Uni
versity.
Thus by the turn of the century, with
the founding of the Delta Corporation,
the relocation of the chapter on the Uni
versity Heights campus, and the comple
tion of the new
Chapter House, the Delta
had basically reached the form in which
it exists today. Frederic Baker, Delta '52,
was the first president of the Delta Corpo
ration in 1898.
During World War I, the Chapter House
was
occupied by the Student Army Train
ing Corp. After the Armistice, the Delta
continued in its prewar growth, thereby
proving, as it had over
fifty years before,
that the Delta was able to survive any
crisis.
During these years strength seemed to
grow from strength. Erik Wallin, Delta
'97, revised the "Yule Log" Ceremony;
Judge Edwin L. Garvin, Delta '97, was
a founder and became the first President
of the Psi Upsilon Alumni Association;
John H. MacCracken, Delta '94, and

In February, 1937, the Delta observed

reopen.
This was

then by the active chapter, who became

Delta and wished them to be continued.
The Chapter House itself was in bad con
dition from deterioration and the damage

45. However, the great generosity of the
alumnis and the work of the active chap
ter have restored over the years the con
dition of the Chapter House, so that it is
now considered the most beautiful and
best maintained fraternity house in the
City of New York.
The alumni and active brethren of the
Delta had not been content with merely
restoring the pre-war condition of the
Chapter, but have endeavored to reeval
uate its role within the community. Critics
of college fraternities have often argued
that college fraternities have ceased to play
a useful role in modem American college
life. The Delta has sought to refute this
falsehood and has tried to show that the
usefulness of college fraternities is not
ending but just beginning.
The Delta is not exclusive but inclusive.
It seeks to take young men of varying
talents and backgrounds and to teach them
how to live and work together and to be
Delta Chapter House
better citizens, not only in college but also
in the years after graduation.
University College is a
large and pos
sible impersonal city university. The Delta
has sought to fill a
gap and to provide
some measure of campus and social life
for its members. A brother of the Delta is
given the chance to form life-long friend
ships and to work and learn in pleasant
and congenial surroundings. He is en
couraged to excel in academic, extra
curricular, and athletic activities, and to
develop his capabilities to the utmost.
The Delta has sought to preserve old
traditions and ritual in a
changing and
uncertain world. The heritage of the past
must not be disregarded but rather should
be utilized for the present and the future.
In the Delta this regard for the traditions
of the past is symbolized by the mainte
nance of rituals which have been respected
for more than a
century.
In these days a
college fraternity can
not exist for itself alone but must work
for the good also of the university or col
lege to which it is attached. It has always
been a
goal of the Delta to make Univer

greater educational institu

have supported it and many have devoted
their lives to teaching its students. The
members of the active chapter are en
